title: Molecular mechanisms and emerging biomarkers of chemical nephrotoxicity: implications for early detection and clinical translation
content:
Abstract
Nephrotoxicity constitutes a formidable clinical and toxicological paradigm, emanating from pharmaceutical agents, environmental xenobiotics, heavy metals, industrial effluents, and naturally occurring toxins. Both acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) manifest through intricate pathophysiological cascades encompassing oxidative stress, mitochondrial derangement, apoptosis, autophagic dysregulation, and inflammatory amplification. Drug-induced kidney injury (DIKI) accounts for nearly one-fifth of nephrotoxicity incidences, yet conventional diagnostic indices—serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen—exhibit limited temporal sensitivity for incipient renal insult. Contemporary biomolecular markers such as: kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), cystatin C, trefoil factor 3 (TFF3), β₂-microglobulin, and osteopontin afford superior precocity and pathotype specificity in detecting nephrotoxic perturbations. Mechanistically, nephrotoxicity ensues from xenobiotic accumulation, transporter-mediated influx, redox disequilibrium, covalent macromolecular adduction, and epigenetic modulation, culminating in tubular and glomerular degeneration. Heavy metals (Hg, Cd, Pb, Cr, U) and environmental pollutants (PM₂.5, PAHs, OPFRs) potentiate oxidative injury and endothelial dysfunction, thereby exacerbating renal pathogenesis. Developmental exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals (BPA, phthalates, PFAS) induces long-term renal vulnerability consistent with the developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) hypothesis. Despite prodigious mechanistic elucidation, translational lacunae persist—particularly regarding chronic low-dose exposures, sex-dependent susceptibility, and multi-toxicant interactions. Integration of omics-based metabolomics, network pharmacology, and organoid or organ-on-chip platforms advances biomarkers validation and stratification. Investigation revealed concerns across contrasting locations, including: an industrial area, bus station, town centre, major urban roadway, and relatively undisturbed rural site. Pharmaceutical adulterants associated to abdominal pain, fatigue, and hypothermia, while BPA was detected in 90% of urine samples.
